paragraphs: 1801. I’ve just come back from visiting my landlord, the one lonely neighbor I’ll have to put up with. This is certainly a beautiful country! I don’t think I could have found a place in all of England so completely removed from the bustle of society. A perfect heaven for a hater of people, and Mr. Heathcliff and I are just the right pair to share the desolation between us. A fine fellow! He little imagined how warmly my heart went out to him when I saw his black eyes retreat so suspiciously under his brows as I rode up, and when his fingers tucked themselves even farther into his waistcoat, with jealous determination, as I announced my name.
“Mr. Heathcliff?” I said.
A nod was the answer.

“Mr. Lockwood, your new tenant, sir. I have the honor of calling as soon as possible after my arrival, to express my hope that I haven’t inconvenienced you by my persistence in asking to take Thrushcross Grange. I heard yesterday that you had had some thoughts—”
“Thrushcross Grange is my own, sir,” he interrupted, wincing. “I wouldn’t allow anyone to inconvenience me if I could prevent it. Walk in!”

The “walk in” was spoken through clenched teeth and expressed the sentiment “Go to the devil!” Even the gate he was leaning on showed no sympathetic movement at the words, and I think that decided me to accept the invitation. I felt interested in a man who seemed even more exaggeratedly reserved than I am.

When he saw my horse’s chest pushing right up against the gate, he did put out his hand to unchain it, and then sullenly led the way up the path, calling out as we entered the yard, “Joseph, take Mr. Lockwood’s horse, and bring up some wine.”
“I suppose this is the entire household staff,” was the thought this double order suggested. “No wonder the grass grows up between the paving stones and cattle are the only hedge trimmers.”

Joseph was an elderly man, no, an old man, perhaps very old, though healthy and sinewy. “The Lord help us!” he muttered in an undertone of peevish displeasure as he took my horse, looking me in the face so sourly that I charitably guessed he must need divine help to digest his dinner, and that his pious exclamation had nothing to do with my unexpected arrival.

Wuthering Heights is the name of Mr. Heathcliff’s home. “Wuthering” is a local word that describes the atmospheric turmoil the house is exposed to in stormy weather. They must certainly have pure, bracing air up there all the time. You can guess the force of the north wind blowing over the edge from the sharp slant of a few stunted firs at the end of the house, and from a row of gaunt thorn trees all stretching their limbs in one direction, as if begging for alms from the sun. Luckily the builder had the foresight to make it strong. The narrow windows are set deep in the wall, and the corners are protected by large jutting stones.

Before crossing the threshold, I paused to admire a quantity of grotesque carving lavished over the front, especially around the main door, above which, among a wilderness of crumbling griffins and shameless little boys, I spotted the date “1500” and the name “Hareton Earnshaw.” I would have made a few comments and asked the surly owner for a short history of the place, but his attitude at the door seemed to demand that I either come in quickly or leave altogether, and I had no wish to add to his impatience before I had seen the inside.

One step took us into the family sitting room, with no entrance hall or passage. Around here they call it simply “the house.” It usually includes both kitchen and parlor, but I believe that at Wuthering Heights the kitchen has been forced to retreat entirely to another part of the building. At least I made out a chatter of voices and a clatter of cooking utensils deep inside, and I saw no sign of roasting, boiling, or baking around the huge fireplace, nor any glitter of copper saucepans and tin strainers on the walls. One end, though, reflected both light and heat splendidly from rows of immense pewter dishes, mixed with silver jugs and tankards, towering row upon row on a vast oak dresser all the way to the roof. The ceiling had never been covered over. Its whole skeleton lay bare to an inquiring eye, except where a wooden rack loaded with oatcakes and bunches of legs of beef, mutton, and ham hid it. Above the chimney were several villainous old guns and a couple of horse pistols, and for decoration three gaudily painted tins stood along its ledge. The floor was of smooth white stone, and the chairs were high-backed, primitive things, painted green, with one or two heavy black ones lurking in the shade. In an arch under the dresser lay a huge liver-colored pointer bitch, surrounded by a swarm of squealing puppies, and other dogs lurked in other corners.

The room and furniture would have been nothing extraordinary for a plain northern farmer, with a stubborn face and strong limbs shown off in knee breeches and gaiters. Such a man, seated in his armchair with his mug of ale frothing on the round table in front of him, can be seen anywhere within five or six miles around these hills, if you go at the right time after dinner. But Mr. Heathcliff forms a striking contrast to his home and way of living. He is dark-skinned like a gypsy in appearance, but in dress and manners a gentleman, that is, as much a gentleman as many a country squire: rather slovenly, perhaps, yet not looking bad for his carelessness, because he has an upright and handsome figure, and rather gloomy. Some people might suspect him of a degree of ill-bred pride. I have a sympathetic feeling inside that tells me it’s nothing of the kind. I know by instinct that his reserve springs from a dislike of showy displays of feeling, of showing mutual kindness. He’ll love and hate equally in secret, and consider it a sort of impertinence to be loved or hated in return. No, I’m running on too fast. I’m giving him too many of my own qualities. Mr. Heathcliff may have entirely different reasons for keeping his hand out of the way when he meets someone who wants to get acquainted, from the ones that drive me. Let me hope my temperament is nearly unique. My dear mother used to say I would never have a comfortable home, and only last summer I proved myself perfectly unworthy of one.

While enjoying a month of fine weather at the seaside, I was thrown into the company of a most fascinating creature, a real goddess in my eyes, as long as she took no notice of me. I never told my love out loud, but if looks have a language, the veriest idiot could have guessed I was head over heels. She understood me at last and gave me a look in return, the sweetest of all imaginable looks. And what did I do? I confess it with shame: I shrank icily into myself like a snail. With every glance I withdrew colder and farther away, until finally the poor innocent girl was led to doubt her own senses and, overwhelmed with embarrassment at her supposed mistake, persuaded her mother to leave.
By this odd twist of character I have gained a reputation for deliberate heartlessness. How undeserved it is, only I can know.

I took a seat at the end of the hearth opposite the one my landlord was heading for, and to fill a silence, I tried to pet the mother dog, who had left her nursery and was creeping up behind my legs like a wolf, with her lip curled and her white teeth watering for a bite. My petting provoked a long, throaty snarl.

“You’d better leave the dog alone,” growled Mr. Heathcliff in unison, checking fiercer displays with a kick of his foot. “She’s not used to being spoiled. She’s not kept as a pet.” Then, striding to a side door, he shouted again, “Joseph!”

Joseph mumbled indistinctly in the depths of the cellar but gave no sign of coming up, so his master dived down to him, leaving me face to face with the ruffian of a bitch and a pair of grim shaggy sheepdogs, who shared with her a jealous watch over all my movements. Not eager to meet their fangs, I sat still. But thinking they would hardly understand silent insults, I unfortunately indulged in winking and making faces at the trio, and some twist of my expression so irritated the lady that she suddenly broke into a fury and leapt on my knees. I flung her back and hurried to put the table between us. This performance roused the whole hive. Half a dozen four-footed fiends of various sizes and ages came out of hidden dens to the common center. I felt my heels and coattails to be special targets of attack, and, fending off the larger combatants as effectively as I could with the poker, I was forced to call out loudly for someone in the household to help restore peace.

Mr. Heathcliff and his man climbed the cellar steps with infuriating calm. I don’t think they moved one second faster than usual, though the hearth was an absolute tempest of snapping and yelping. Fortunately, someone in the kitchen moved faster. A sturdy woman with her skirt tucked up, bare arms, and cheeks flushed from the fire rushed into the middle of us, waving a frying pan. She used that weapon, and her tongue, to such effect that the storm subsided as if by magic, and she was left alone, heaving like a sea after a high wind, when her master came onto the scene.
“What the devil is the matter?” he asked, eyeing me in a way I could hardly endure after such inhospitable treatment.

“What the devil, indeed!” I muttered. “The herd of possessed pigs couldn’t have had worse spirits in them than those animals of yours, sir. You might as well leave a stranger with a litter of tigers!”
“They won’t bother people who touch nothing,” he remarked, putting the bottle in front of me and setting the displaced table back in place. “The dogs are right to be watchful. Have a glass of wine?”
“No, thank you.”
“You’re not bitten, are you?”
“If I had been, I’d have put my mark on the biter.” Heathcliff’s face relaxed into a grin.

“Come, come,” he said, “you’re flustered, Mr. Lockwood. Here, take a little wine. Guests are so exceedingly rare in this house that I and my dogs, I’m willing to admit, hardly know how to receive them. Your health, sir?”

I bowed and returned the toast, beginning to see that it would be foolish to sit sulking over the misbehavior of a pack of curs. Besides, I was reluctant to give the man any more amusement at my expense, since his humor was taking that turn. Probably swayed by the practical consideration that it would be foolish to offend a good tenant, he relaxed a little his clipped habit of dropping pronouns and auxiliary verbs, and brought up what he supposed would interest me: a discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of my present place of retirement. I found him very intelligent on the topics we touched on, and before I went home I was encouraged enough to offer another visit tomorrow. He clearly doesn’t want my intrusion repeated. I shall go anyway. It’s astonishing how sociable I feel compared with him.
